title: Anna Howard Shaw Day

jokes.text: 'Valentine's Day is a sham created by card companies to reinforce and exploit gender stereotypes.' — immediately followed by 'Tommy Reticker gave me a card. I like Valentine's Day.'
jokes.setup: Liz delivers a confident feminist anti-Valentine's speech
jokes.punchline: The child immediately undercuts it with simple, pure enthusiasm: a boy gave her a card
jokes.explanation: Beautifully economic. Liz's high-minded feminist rant is demolished in six words by a child. The structural contrast between Liz's elaborate cynicism and Evelyn's simple joy is well-executed. The economy score is nearly perfect — not a single wasted word.

jokes.text: 'Learn from my sexual misadventures, Evelyn.'
jokes.setup: Liz is trying to give child-appropriate advice
jokes.punchline: She frames her romantic disasters as 'sexual misadventures' while addressing a young girl
jokes.explanation: The word 'misadventures' is doing enormous heavy lifting — it's clinical enough to be funny, and 'sexual' applied to Liz's sad romantic life is perfectly self-deprecating. The choice to address a child as a peer in romantic failure is very Liz Lemon.

jokes.text: 'Last Valentine's Day, I watched my boyfriend, Drew's, mother/grandmother die.'
jokes.setup: Liz is listing her Valentine's Day disasters
jokes.punchline: The 'mother/grandmother' construction implies an incestuous family situation while also being a horrifying thing to witness on Valentine's Day
jokes.explanation: The 'mother/grandmother' slash is a callback to a previous season's storyline that rewards long-time viewers (rewatch bonus), but also lands on its own as an absurd hyphenation suggesting family dysfunction. The casual way Liz delivers it mid-list makes it funnier. One of the episode's stronger jokes in the opening.

jokes.text: 'I met Floyd on Valentine's Day, but he left me for the city of Cleveland.'
jokes.setup: Liz is listing Valentine's disasters; we expect another person-related failure
jokes.punchline: The rival for Floyd's affections was an entire American city, not another woman
jokes.explanation: The personification of Cleveland as a romantic rival is funny and absurdist. The phrasing 'left me for the city of Cleveland' perfectly captures Liz's self-pitying framing of a normal relocation decision as a personal betrayal.

jokes.text: 'And forget about Dennis. That pervert would always just try to get me drunk.'
jokes.setup: The list of Valentine's disasters has escalated from death to city-rivalry
jokes.punchline: Dennis is dismissed as simply 'that pervert' who tried to get her drunk — so normalized that Liz says it to a child without hesitation
jokes.explanation: Dennis Duffy is a recurring character whose awfulness is well-established, so this lands for regular viewers. The joke is the casual normalizing of his behavior. Slightly weaker than the others in the sequence because it relies entirely on prior character knowledge.

jokes.text: Liz buys cookies but reframes them as celebrating 'the February 14th birthday of Anna Howard Shaw, famed American suffragette'
jokes.setup: Liz refuses to buy cookies for Valentine's Day on principle
jokes.punchline: She buys them anyway but invents an elaborate alternative justification to avoid admitting she wants Valentine's Day cookies
jokes.explanation: This is a near-perfect Liz Lemon joke. Her desperate intellectualization of a simple desire (she wants cookies on Valentine's Day) via an obscure historical figure is exactly who she is. The name 'Anna Howard Shaw' is inherently funny — specific enough to be real, obscure enough to be absurd. It becomes the episode's title and running gag. The 'famed American suffragette' qualifier is especially funny because it's the kind of thing only Liz would say to a child. Justifies the 8+ score.

jokes.text: 'Happy Anna Howard Shaw Day to us all!' — Liz says triumphantly to the hall
jokes.setup: Liz has just convinced herself (and no one else) that buying Valentine's cookies is actually about Anna Howard Shaw
jokes.punchline: She announces it to the building like it's an accepted holiday, fully committed to the bit
jokes.explanation: The full commitment to the fake holiday, announced as if it's a real cultural moment, is the comedic escalation that makes joke #7 land even harder in retrospect. The episode title paying off immediately in the cold open is elegant structure.

jokes.text: Jack asks Liz which tie is more attractive for a TV appearance — the red — 'Thank you. I've got to look camera ready tonight.'
jokes.setup: Jack treats Liz as a trusted advisor on how to appear sexually appealing on camera
jokes.punchline: The implicit joke is that Liz's taste is deeply questionable and Jack consulting her about attraction is inherently misguided, yet he takes her advice immediately
jokes.explanation: A functional character-dynamic joke. The humor is in Jack treating Liz as a useful authority on sexual attractiveness. Not especially original but well-executed as a scene-opener.

jokes.text: 'No, C.N.B.C. gives me a headache. I get all my money advice from P.B.S. — Where should I put my money? In tech stocks? Or the housing market? — Tech stocks, Foxy Moneybags! Tech stocks!'
jokes.setup: Jack mentions The Hot Box on CNBC; Liz says she gets money advice from PBS
jokes.punchline: PBS financial advice apparently involves a character called 'Foxy Moneybags' giving extremely enthusiastic stock tips
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's standout jokes. 'Foxy Moneybags' as the name of a PBS financial advisor is perfectly absurd — it's a children's show character name applied to personal finance. The rapid delivery of the full PBS show exchange, performed entirely by Liz doing both roles, is excellent comedic economy. The specificity ('tech stocks!' twice) elevates it beyond a simple absurdist name joke. Justifies the 8+ score: it's a fully realized absurdist bit in three lines.

jokes.text: No, C.N.B.C. gives me a headache. I get all my money advice from P.B.S. / Where should I put my money? In tech stocks? Or the housing market? / Tech stocks, Foxy Moneybags! Tech stocks!
jokes.setup: Liz says she gets financial advice from PBS instead of CNBC.
jokes.punchline: The PBS financial advisor turns out to be a cartoonish character called 'Foxy Moneybags' shouting simplistic advice with bizarre enthusiasm.
jokes.explanation: This is a genuine standout joke. The name 'Foxy Moneybags' alone is brilliant — it implies a children's-show aesthetic applied to adult finance. The shouted 'Tech stocks!' followed by 'Tech stocks!' is perfectly paced absurdist escalation. High originality, very quotable, classic 30 Rock cutaway construction. 'Foxy Moneybags' is a character who deserved a spinoff.

jokes.text: Jack's assistant Jonathan asks 'are you and I exchanging...' — Jack cuts him off with 'No.'
jokes.setup: Jonathan is setting up Valentine's Day reservations for Jack and attempts to ask about their own dynamic
jokes.punchline: Jack shuts it down instantly before Jonathan can finish the sentence, implying Jonathan has romantic feelings that are completely unwelcome
jokes.explanation: Economy score is nearly perfect — the entire joke is one word. Jack's 'No' before Jonathan finishes speaking tells us everything about Jonathan's unrequited devotion and Jack's complete indifference. A running character dynamic delivered with maximum compression.

jokes.text: Jack's description of the intensity of Nancy: 'Like when you think there's one more stair, but there isn't. And all of a sudden, you're like "Whoa!"'
jokes.setup: Jack is describing how emotionally intense and disorienting his relationship with Nancy was
jokes.punchline: He compares a complex, intense romantic history to the mundane physical sensation of misjudging a staircase
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. The bathetic comparison — taking a profound romantic entanglement and equating it to the disorienting sensation of a missing stair step — is genuinely original. Jack's deadpan commitment to the metaphor ('Exactly.' from Liz) makes it land even harder. The image is so specific and universal that it becomes immediately quotable. Justifies 8+: it's a fully original comedic concept delivered with perfect economy and character voice.

jokes.text: 'Frankly, I could use a win.' / 'A win? What's with the euphemisms, Jack? Why don't you just say you want some...' / 'Is that sex, Lemon?' / 'It's the way I do it.'
jokes.setup: Jack says he 'could use a win'; Liz suggests he's being euphemistic about wanting sex
jokes.punchline: Jack's confused 'Is that sex, Lemon?' implies Liz's version of sex sounds so strange that he needs confirmation, and 'It's the way I do it' is the perfect self-own
jokes.explanation: The exchange flips the usual dynamic: normally Jack is worldly and Liz is naive, but here Liz's description of sex sounds so alien to Jack that he has to ask for clarification. 'It's the way I do it' is a perfect Liz Lemon self-deprecating punchline. High character integration — this works because of the specific Liz/Jack dynamic.

jokes.text: Jack's date system: Jonathan calls with a fake 'conference call with the Geneva office'; if Jack likes the date, he 'loudly tells Jonathan' he's doing something more important, the woman is 'suitably impressed,' and Jack is 'guaranteed to see some underwear. Perhaps a bra with a front clasp.'
jokes.setup: Jack explains his elaborate system for first dates
jokes.punchline: The escalating specificity ends with the very specific goal of 'a bra with a front clasp' — the precision of the detail is funnier than any general lewdness would be
jokes.explanation: The 'bra with a front clasp' is a wonderfully specific and unexpected endpoint for what began as a business-speak description of a dating strategy. The joke works because Jack treats romantic conquest with the same systematic, corporate precision he applies to everything. The specificity of the front clasp detail elevates it.

jokes.text: Liz: 'I scheduled a root canal for February 14th, Jack. I will spend half the day in twilight sleep. Then I will go home and watch the Lifetime original movie, My Stepson is My Cyber-Husband.'
jokes.setup: Jack asks about Liz's Valentine's Day plans
jokes.punchline: She has not only preemptively avoided Valentine's Day with dental surgery but has planned a specific, horrifying Lifetime movie to cap the evening
jokes.explanation: A masterclass in Liz Lemon character comedy. The layering is exceptional: she's (1) actively scheduled surgery to avoid the holiday, (2) framed unconsciousness as a leisure activity, and (3) planned a follow-up Lifetime movie whose title is its own joke. 'My Stepson is My Cyber-Husband' is a perfectly calibrated fake Lifetime title — it hits every Lifetime movie trope (family scandal, internet peril) while being completely absurd. The character integration is nearly perfect: only Liz Lemon would do all three of these things. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: 'Wow, that is inspired. You are truly the Picasso of loneliness.'
jokes.setup: Jack has just heard Liz's elaborate plan to avoid Valentine's Day via dental surgery and a horrifying Lifetime movie
jokes.punchline: He responds with genuine, awed admiration — calling her the 'Picasso of loneliness' frames her misery as a form of mastery
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'The Picasso of loneliness' is genuinely brilliant — it frames Liz's elaborate avoidance of love as a form of artistic genius, which is simultaneously a savage insult and a sincere compliment given Jack's respect for excellence. The economy is near-perfect (six words, maximum payload). The line is immediately quotable and has become a cultural reference for the show. Justifies 8+: it's the kind of line that defines a character and an episode simultaneously.

jokes.text: Liz's comeback: 'Or I am that painting elephant of being awesome.'
jokes.setup: Jack has just called her 'the Picasso of loneliness'
jokes.punchline: Liz tries to counter with the famous elephant that makes abstract art, but the construction is so garbled it becomes its own joke
jokes.explanation: A good callback that adds a layer to joke #16. Liz's attempt to reclaim the Picasso comparison by invoking the painting elephant is funny because the sentence structure itself is broken ('that painting elephant of being awesome' is grammatically wrong in a way that sounds exactly like how Liz would fumble a comeback). It's a character joke about Liz being unable to articulate her own defense.

jokes.text: Jenna reveals her stalker sends her Valentine's Day gifts and is concerned because she hasn't heard from him
jokes.setup: Kenneth asks if Jenna has received packages
jokes.punchline: The package she's waiting for is from her stalker, 'Maynard Roger Hoynes,' and she's distressed by his silence
jokes.explanation: The inversion — celebrity distressed that her stalker hasn't been in touch — is a strong premise. Sets up the B-plot effectively. Jenna's narcissism makes this character-specific.

jokes.text: 'It's a real problem in the celebrity community. But if Beyonce simply answered one of my letters, I'd stop trying to break into her house.'
jokes.setup: Jenna is explaining that stalking is a problem for celebrities
jokes.punchline: She reveals she herself stalks Beyonce, completely undermining her victim framing
jokes.explanation: A genuinely clever structural inversion: Jenna begins as a victim (has a stalker) but is immediately revealed to be a perpetrator (stalks Beyonce). The logic of 'if she just answered my letters I'd stop breaking in' is perfect narcissistic reasoning. The Beyonce specificity grounds it in reality while keeping it absurd. Justifies 8+: the setup-inversion-callback structure in three sentences is tight comedic writing.

jokes.text: 'Maynard's debilitating devotion validates how wonderful I am.'
jokes.setup: Kenneth asks if no contact from the stalker is actually a good thing
jokes.punchline: Jenna explains the stalker's value to her self-image in a single perfectly articulated sentence
jokes.explanation: The word 'debilitating' is doing extraordinary work here — it acknowledges the stalker's dysfunction while framing it as a feature, not a bug. The sentence is a perfectly compressed portrait of Jenna's narcissism. 'Validates how wonderful I am' is the punchline and character thesis simultaneously. Justifies 8+: perfect economy, deep character integration, and the word choice ('debilitating') elevates it above a simple narcissism joke.

jokes.text: But what does it say about me if he's moved on? Maybe to one of my peers, like Julia Roberts.
jokes.setup: Jenna is upset that her stalker might have lost interest.
jokes.punchline: She frames her stalker potentially moving to another target as professional competition — and casually names Julia Roberts as her peer.
jokes.explanation: Jenna's casual self-comparison to Julia Roberts while treating stalker competition as a professional metric is perfectly calibrated narcissism. The stakes (losing a stalker) are treated with the gravity of losing a film role.

jokes.text: Frank casually asks the writers' room if they know any 'cool, new sex positions' for his 'girlfriend' Karen's Valentine's visit
jokes.setup: Frank asks the room about sex positions for Valentine's Day
jokes.punchline: The subsequent revelation that Karen is widely believed not to exist makes the request retroactively sad and absurd
jokes.explanation: A setup joke that mostly exists to establish the Karen running gag. The 'caliente' word choice is mildly funny but the real joke is the immediate skeptical response from the room.

jokes.text: 'Oh, my God, Lutz. Are you still pretending Karen exists?' / 'She's real. Would a fake woman have a personal website at JDLutz.com/karen/proof?'
jokes.setup: The room doesn't believe Lutz's girlfriend Karen exists
jokes.punchline: Lutz's defense — she has a website specifically called '/karen/proof' — is funnier than any denial could be, because only someone trying to fabricate a girlfriend would create that URL
jokes.explanation: The specific URL 'JDLutz.com/karen/proof' is genuinely brilliant comedy writing. The existence of a website dedicated to proving a girlfriend is real is inherently suspicious and pathetic. The 'proof' subdirectory is the cherry on top — no one with a real girlfriend would do this. A perfect absurdist detail that's also deeply character-specific. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Another writer: 'My cousin set me up on a blind date for Valentine's, and I just found out the girl is... well, urban.' — 'Are you saying she's black?'
jokes.setup: A writer is trying to use a euphemism to explain his discomfort with a blind date
jokes.punchline: The direct translation ('Are you saying she's black?') exposes the racism of the euphemism by refusing to let it slide
jokes.explanation: A functional joke that calls out coded language. The humor is in the directness of calling out the euphemism. Less inventive than the surrounding material — the premise (calling out coded racism) is well-worn territory, though it works in context.

jokes.text: Toofer's Valentine's Day solution: go out with Frank and a janitor with 'messed-up teeth' who 'will only go out with me if she can bring her ugly sister'
jokes.setup: Toofer doesn't know how to get out of his blind date
jokes.punchline: Frank's alternative is profoundly sad: a date with a janitor whose condition is bringing her 'ugly sister'
jokes.explanation: A dark joke about the depressing Valentine's Day alternatives available to the writers' room. Functional but not particularly clever — relies on the sad image rather than wit.

jokes.text: Wow, I can't believe you guys are letting Valentine's Day win. Not me. One word. Oral. / Two words. Oral surgery. I'm having oral surgery and skipping Valentine's Day. Doctor's orders.
jokes.setup: Liz reacts to the writers' pathetic Valentine's plans.
jokes.punchline: The pause after 'Oral' creates a deliberate misdirection before the punchline 'surgery' lands. Liz's triumphant self-correction ('two words') makes it even better.
jokes.explanation: Textbook misdirection executed with perfect structure. The beat between 'Oral' and 'surgery' is essential — the audience fills in one word and gets a completely different one. The meta-joke of Liz being wrong about the number of words ('one word... two words') is a beautiful self-aware addition that shows the writers understanding their own construction. One of the tightest joke structures in the episode.

jokes.text: 'Wow, I can't believe you guys are letting Valentine's Day win.' / 'Not me. One word. Oral.' / 'Two words. Oral surgery. I'm having oral surgery and skipping Valentine's Day. Doctor's orders.'
jokes.setup: Liz criticizes the writers for avoiding Valentine's Day; someone says 'One word. Oral.'
jokes.punchline: After a deliberately suggestive pause, Liz completes it as 'oral surgery' — but the 'two words' correction is the punchline within the punchline
jokes.explanation: The fake-out ('One word. Oral.') followed by 'Two words. Oral surgery.' is a well-structured misdirection. But the real joke is the '...two words' correction — Liz is so committed to her bit that she even corrects the grammar of her own punchline setup. The pedantry is perfectly Liz.

jokes.text: Doctor's rules: someone must pick Liz up after anesthesia. Pete shares: 'When I had my wisdom teeth out, I tried to get in the bath with my mom.'
jokes.setup: Pete is warning Liz about how anesthesia messes you up
jokes.punchline: His personal example is deeply Freudian and horrifying — attempting to join his mother in the bath while post-anesthesia
jokes.explanation: A good dark joke that works on two levels: it's a genuine warning about anesthesia effects, AND Pete's specific example is so inappropriately Freudian that it becomes the joke. The delivery (matter-of-fact) is essential — Pete seems to have made peace with this memory.

jokes.text: Pete's Valentine's Day tradition: 'Every year, Paula and I rent this big suite up at Niagara. Then she takes the kids there and I stay home and get wasted in my garage. It's what keeps the magic alive.'
jokes.setup: Liz asks Pete if he's free to pick her up on Valentine's Day
jokes.punchline: Pete's 'tradition' is his wife going on vacation without him while he gets drunk alone in his garage, and he frames this as the secret to a happy marriage
jokes.explanation: The gradual reveal structure is excellent: 'big suite at Niagara' sounds romantic, then 'she takes the kids there' reverses expectations, then 'I stay home and get wasted in my garage' completes the inversion. 'It's what keeps the magic alive' is the deadpan capper that frames profound marital dysfunction as relationship wisdom. Strong Pete character integration — this is exactly the sad life Pete leads.

jokes.text: Avery Jessup's immediate skewering of Walter Stein: 'Also joining me, Walter Stein, whose bow tie tells us he works for some liberal think tank. And the food in his beard tells us that he purchased a snack pack on the train from New Haven.'
jokes.setup: Avery introduces her panel guests on The Hot Box
jokes.punchline: She reads Walter's entire sad existence from his bow tie and beard food in two sentences
jokes.explanation: A brilliant character introduction for Avery: in two sentences she demonstrates intelligence, cruelty, and wit. The 'food in his beard' detail is both specific and devastating. The 'snack pack on the train from New Haven' tells us Walter's entire life trajectory (Yale liberal academic commuter) via a single inference. Justifies 8+: maximum information density, perfect economy, excellent character establishment.

jokes.text: The Hot Box rapid-fire Q&A: 'Who will be the next President?' / 'Mitt Romney's oldest son, Jezba.' / 'Dennis Kucinich.' / 'Okay, that's sad, Walter. Just sad.'
jokes.setup: The show plays a rapid-fire game; everyone gives quick answers
jokes.punchline: Jack's answer is an invented Romney son named 'Jezba' (absurd but plausible-ish); Walter's sincere answer of Dennis Kucinich gets genuine pity from Avery
jokes.explanation: The name 'Jezba' is funny because it sounds vaguely Mormon-ish but is clearly fabricated — it satirizes both the Romney brand of politics and the show's fictional universe. Kucinich being the punchline (as a real politician used as a symbol of hopeless idealism) lands because Avery's reaction ('that's sad, Walter') is so precise.

jokes.text: Jack: 'Blackberry, Warren Buffett. iPhone, Jimmy Buffett.' — speed dial answers
jokes.setup: Avery asks who's on Jack's speed dial
jokes.punchline: The two phones have the two Buffetts — the financial genius and the beach bum musician — as the contrast punchline
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy — four words deliver the punchline. The joke works because both people are plausibly on Jack's speed dial: Warren Buffett for business, Jimmy Buffett for... the other side of Jack that loves kitsch Americana. The parallel structure is perfect. Near-perfect economy score.

jokes.text: Jack's favorite movie: 'Tie, The Fountainhead or Uncle Buck.'
jokes.setup: Avery asks Jack's favorite movie
jokes.punchline: The pairing of Ayn Rand's hyper-individualist manifesto with a John Hughes family comedy is so unexpected it's perfect character revelation
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best character jokes. 'The Fountainhead' is exactly the movie Jack would claim; 'Uncle Buck' is the movie Jack would actually love. The combination reveals his contradictions — the high-minded plutocrat with a secret sentimental streak — in four words. The word 'tie' refuses to prioritize one over the other, making it funnier. This is how you establish a complex character in a punchline. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Walter volunteers his movie: 'My wife and I just saw The Yellow Handkerchief.' / Avery: 'Just sit a couple out, Stein, god.'
jokes.setup: The rapid-fire game doesn't ask Walter for his answer
jokes.punchline: Walter volunteers anyway with an aggressively unappealing art film; Avery's dismissal is perfectly contemptuous
jokes.explanation: Avery's 'Just sit a couple out, Stein, god' is great — the dismissive use of his surname and the exasperated 'god' make it feel like genuine contempt. Walter as a running punching bag is well-executed and reveals Avery's character efficiently.

jokes.text: Jack and Avery bond over karaoke: Jack does Nitty Gritty Dirt Band; Avery 'rocks the brothers Halen' — 'Let's grab a drink after this.' / 'You read my mind.'
jokes.setup: The karaoke question is meant to reveal character; both give surprising but perfect answers
jokes.punchline: Avery's 'brothers Halen' (Van Halen) and Jack's Nitty Gritty Dirt Band are both unexpected and perfectly reveal their characters; the instant romantic connection is the payoff
jokes.explanation: A functional romantic-comedy beat that doubles as character revelation. 'Brothers Halen' is slightly funnier than it needs to be (the formality of 'the brothers Halen' for Van Halen is absurdist). The instant mutual attraction is efficient but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Tracy's Valentine's Day: 'Angie and I rent a room with a heart-shaped hot tub and cook chili in it. Then we take it to a soup kitchen. And that's where it starts to get sexy.'
jokes.setup: Liz asks Tracy for a ride on Valentine's Day; he has plans
jokes.punchline: The escalation from 'heart-shaped hot tub chili' (already absurd) to 'we take it to a soup kitchen' (genuinely charitable) to 'and that's where it starts to get sexy' (inexplicable) is a three-beat absurdist masterpiece
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode. Three beats, each weirder than the last, building to a punchline that is simultaneously charitable, absurd, and completely inexplicable. The genius is the 'that's where it starts to get sexy' — the soup kitchen is somehow the romantic part. This is calibrated Tracy Jordan absurdism at its finest: each element is unexpected, the escalation is perfect, and the final beat defies any logical explanation. The chili-in-hot-tub detail is specific enough to be real but wrong enough to be funny. This approaches the 'Snip snap' anchor in quality. Justifies 9+.

jokes.text: Can't talk, Liz. I just got my stalker's work address from his parole officer, and I'm going to confront him about why he's ignoring me.
jokes.setup: Liz asks Jenna for Valentine's help.
jokes.punchline: Jenna has obtained her stalker's address through his parole officer and plans to confront him about ignoring her — treating the predator/prey dynamic completely backwards.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'I'd stop breaking into Beyoncé's house' to 'I got my stalker's address from his parole officer' is a perfect callback development. The role reversal — stalker confronting stalkee — is well-executed. Strong character work.

jokes.text: Kenneth's Valentine's Day plans: 'I will be attending an all-day abstinence rally. You're welcome to come. I think I've got an extra gender-neutralizing hood.'
jokes.setup: Liz asks Kenneth if he's free on Valentine's Day
jokes.punchline: The abstinence rally has a 'gender-neutralizing hood' as standard equipment — the specificity of the hood transforms this from a standard religious joke into something much weirder
jokes.explanation: The 'gender-neutralizing hood' is a stroke of absurdist specificity. Kenneth earnestly inviting Liz and mentioning he has a spare hood suggests these are standard-issue at the rally, which is horrifying and funny. The term 'gender-neutralizing' applied to a physical garment is the kind of absurd-but-internally-logical detail that distinguishes great comedy writing. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Liz passes someone in the hall: 'Hey, Liz!' / 'Hey.' / 'The answer's no.'
jokes.setup: Someone calls out to Liz in the hall
jokes.punchline: Before they can even ask anything, Liz preemptively says 'The answer's no' — she's so exhausted from being asked for Valentine's Day favors she's now refusing in advance
jokes.explanation: A quick beat that works through extreme economy. The comedy is entirely in the timing — 'Hey.' / 'The answer's no.' We don't know what was going to be asked, making it funnier. Also escalates the running joke of everyone having Valentine's plans that need Liz's help.

jokes.text: Jenna confronts her stalker Maynard: 'Has the dog who gives you your orders died?' / 'No, Brandon's fine.'
jokes.setup: Jenna asks why Maynard has been ignoring her; she assumes the worst — that the dog commanding him has died
jokes.punchline: 'Brandon's fine' — the stalker confirms the dog commander is alive and well, treating it as an entirely reasonable question
jokes.explanation: A Son of Sam reference (the 'dog who gives orders') that's both a deep cut and immediately legible. What makes it exceptional is Maynard's earnest confirmation — 'No, Brandon's fine' — treating the question as completely normal. The stalker has a dog named Brandon who gives him orders and he sees no issue with this. The economy of the exchange is perfect. Justifies 8+: the joke requires cultural knowledge but pays off enormously for those who have it, and Maynard's straight answer elevates it.

jokes.text: Maynard tells Jenna he's quitting stalking her: 'I have a new therapist. I'm taking my meds. I can't even see electricity shooting out of your head anymore.'
jokes.setup: Maynard says he's getting better and can no longer stalk Jenna
jokes.punchline: His measure of mental health improvement is that he can no longer see electricity coming from Jenna's head — framed as a loss rather than a gain
jokes.explanation: The 'electricity shooting out of your head' detail is specific, visual, and weird in exactly the right way. What makes it land is the implication that Maynard mourns losing his delusion — the medication is working, but it's taken something away. The joke works on the character level (Jenna is upset he can no longer see her supernatural quality) and on the dark comedy level (antipsychotics eliminating a hallucination described as a gift). Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: 'I always knew this would end someday. I just thought it would be with me in the trunk of a rental car.'
jokes.setup: Jenna accepts that Maynard is ending the stalking relationship
jokes.punchline: Her romantic ideal for how the relationship would end was being kidnapped in a rental car trunk — she's disappointed this is ending with a conversation instead
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. The 'rental car' specification is perfect — a purchased car would be too committed, but a rental suggests the stalker even tried to be economically responsible about kidnapping. Jenna's disappointment that she won't get to be in a trunk is the darkest possible expression of her narcissism: she wanted to be kidnapped because being the object of that much effort would validate her. The economy is near-perfect. This is in the upper tier of the episode's jokes. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Jack's date: 'Choate, then Yale, then two years in Africa with the Peace Corp.' / 'The Peace Corps, that's surprising.' / 'Oh, no, The Peace Corp. Lawrence Peace's corporation. We drilled for oil in gorilla habitats.'
jokes.setup: Jack's date mentions 'the Peace Corp' — Jack mishears/assumes it's The Peace Corps, the humanitarian organization
jokes.punchline: It's Lawrence Peace's corporation, which drills for oil in gorilla habitats — the opposite of humanitarian
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed misdirection. The setup lulls us into thinking she's admirable (Peace Corps), then the reveal is a satirical double inversion: it sounds humanitarian (Peace Corp) but is the most anti-humanitarian thing possible (oil drilling in gorilla habitats). The name 'Lawrence Peace' is funny because it's a plausible name that makes the company name sound legitimate. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Jack casually mentions he 'learned to talk to gorillas when I worked for G.E. Medical. We are going to test poisons on you.'
jokes.setup: Jack responds to hearing about gorilla habitats by sharing his gorilla experience
jokes.punchline: His gorilla-language proficiency apparently involves telling them they're poison test subjects — a horrifying corporate confession delivered as small talk
jokes.explanation: The joke works on multiple levels: Jack's corporate history at GE (a real company being satirized), the absurdity of learning gorilla sign language specifically to inform gorillas of their fate, and the casual delivery of 'We are going to test poisons on you' as if it's a pleasant anecdote. The period-like sentence 'We are going to test poisons on you' as gorilla-speak is brilliantly specific. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Jack's date: 'I think it started when I walked in on my parents doing it the day Reagan was shot.' / Jack: 'I wouldn't over-analyze that.'
jokes.setup: Jack's date explains her attraction to 'commanding salt-and-pepper types' by tracing it to a childhood trauma
jokes.punchline: Walking in on parents having sex the day of an assassination attempt is so specific and disturbing that Jack's therapeutic non-advice ('I wouldn't over-analyze that') becomes the understatement punchline
jokes.explanation: The comedy requires two things happening simultaneously: (1) an extremely specific traumatic childhood memory that is also historically specific, and (2) Jack's massive underreaction. 'I wouldn't over-analyze that' is perfect deadpan — it both dismisses the obvious psychological content and reveals Jack's unwillingness to engage emotionally. The Reagan specificity elevates it above a generic Freud joke.

jokes.text: One time, I ran over an old lady in Arizona and just kept driving.
jokes.setup: The date has just declared 'I love having secrets with you' in response to Jonathan's call — she's sharing intimacy
jokes.punchline: Her idea of sharing a secret is casual vehicular manslaughter confession, delivered as pillow-talk-equivalent
jokes.explanation: A good dark comedy moment — the intimacy escalation of 'I love having secrets' is immediately undercut by this woman's 'secret' being actual crime. The Arizona specificity is funny. Economy is high: one sentence, maximum impact.

jokes.text: Avery sees through the conference call move: 'It's 3:30 in the morning in Geneva, Jack. Who's your call with? The hooker working the corner outside Raiffeisenbank?'
jokes.setup: Jack deploys his fake Geneva conference call on Avery
jokes.punchline: Avery immediately exposes it with time-zone math AND specifies the precise location of the Swiss sex worker — the specificity of 'Raiffeisenbank' is the comedy
jokes.explanation: An excellent callback payoff. The joke works because Avery is so specifically knowledgeable (Swiss time zones, actual Swiss banks) that she can demolish Jack's move while also being funnier than he is. 'Raiffeisenbank' is a real Swiss bank, and its use as a landmark for a sex worker is perfectly absurd. The callback structure (establishing the move, then having it fail on the smartest character) rewards the episode's architecture. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Jack's recovery: 'Well, it is February. And in Switzerland, that is, uh, "Night Business Month".'
jokes.setup: Avery has demolished Jack's conference call move; he tries to recover
jokes.punchline: He invents 'Night Business Month' as a Swiss cultural practice — clearly improvised and completely ridiculous, but delivered with enough Donaghy confidence to almost work
jokes.explanation: 'Night Business Month' is a perfectly Jack Donaghy fabrication — it sounds corporate enough to be real, and the 'uh' before it reveals he's making it up in real time. The character integration is excellent: only Jack would try to brazen out an exposed lie with an invented Swiss custom.

jokes.text: Avery: 'Look at me, Jack. Look how my body goes with this dress. I don't need to be dealing with amateurs.'
jokes.setup: Jack's 'Night Business Month' excuse has failed; Avery rejects him
jokes.punchline: Her dismissal is simultaneously a self-compliment ('my body goes with this dress') and a put-down — she's too good-looking to waste time on someone using old tricks
jokes.explanation: 'Look how my body goes with this dress' is an unusual phrasing that's funnier than a straightforward 'I'm beautiful' — it's almost architectural. The confidence is specific to Avery as a character. Her self-assessment as too good for amateurs establishes her as Jack's equal, which is important for the romantic subplot.

jokes.text: Frank's Valentine's plans: 'That cleaning lady finally agreed to go out with me. We're going to pick up some pierogies and then eat them at her husband's grave.'
jokes.setup: Liz asks Frank if he's free on Valentine's Day
jokes.punchline: The date plan involves both pierogies AND the husband's grave — the specificity of pierogies as the food choice AND the graveside setting creates layers of sad comedy
jokes.explanation: The combination of pierogies and eating them at the dead husband's grave is a wonderfully specific dark comedy detail. The pierogies are the right cultural/demographic detail for the cleaning lady character without being demeaning; the husband's grave turns the date from merely sad to genuinely dark. The specificity elevates this above a generic 'pathetic date' joke. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Frank's taunt: 'You thought you were so much smarter than us, didn't you? But now, you're in the exact same crappy Valentine's Day boat everyone else is in.'
jokes.setup: Liz asks Frank for a ride home from surgery, he's busy
jokes.punchline: Frank turns the tables on Liz, pointing out that her elaborate root canal plan has the same core problem as everyone else's situation — she's also alone on Valentine's Day
jokes.explanation: A thematic beat more than a joke — it states the episode's thesis directly. Functional but not particularly clever. The 'crappy Valentine's Day boat' metaphor is fine but not memorable.

jokes.text: 'In fact, yours is worse. If you don't get that tooth fixed, the infection will probably move to your brain and kill you.'
jokes.setup: Frank has just told Liz her situation is equivalent to everyone else's
jokes.punchline: He escalates: actually, hers is worse, because an untreated tooth infection could be fatal — and he delivers this as the final item in his argument
jokes.explanation: A functional dark escalation. The medical fact (tooth infections can spread to the brain) deployed as a Valentine's Day insult is a good tone combination. Not especially original but competently executed.

jokes.text: Liz: 'Yeah, well, if I die, my ghost is going to haunt you.' / Frank: 'Then your ghost is going to see some disgusting stuff.'
jokes.setup: Liz threatens to haunt Frank if she dies from the tooth infection
jokes.punchline: Frank's response reframes the haunting as a punishment for Liz's ghost — implying whatever he does at home is too disgusting for even a ghost to witness
jokes.explanation: A nicely inverted comeback. The joke transforms the haunting threat into something that hurts Liz's ghost more than Frank — and the implication about what Frank does privately is funnier for being vague. The structure is elegant: threat → counterthreat that also establishes character.

jokes.text: Avery sent Jack a watch set to Geneva time as a 'next move'; the note reads 'hopefully you won't make the same mistake again, mon se poivre' — 'That means "my salt and pepper" in Swiss French.'
jokes.setup: Avery rejected Jack last night but followed up with a gift
jokes.punchline: 'Mon se poivre' is not French (it's not 'Swiss French' either — the phrase doesn't exist), and describing it as 'Swiss French' is either Jack being wrong or the show being self-aware about invented language
jokes.explanation: The 'Swiss French' designation is the joke — it's either Jack not knowing French, or Avery being playful. Either way, the salt-and-pepper callback to Jack's appearance is a nice character moment. Moderate craft score because the joke is pleasant but not particularly inventive.

jokes.text: 'She was on Maxim's "I'd Rape That 100"'
jokes.setup: Liz comments on Avery Jessup being hot
jokes.punchline: Maxim's list is given a name so offensive it becomes a satire of lad mag culture — the list name itself is the joke
jokes.explanation: A deliberately provocative joke that satirizes Maxim-style objectification by naming the list what those publications were effectively saying implicitly. The joke is the exaggeration making the subtext text. Some viewers will find this edgy-funny, others will find it too dark. The economy is good; the character integration is weak (this line could be said by anyone).

jokes.text: 'The male escort that I hired to take me home from surgery has had a chlamydia flare-up'
jokes.setup: Liz reveals her backup plan for getting home from surgery
jokes.punchline: She hired a male escort for a nonsexual purpose (transportation), but the 'chlamydia flare-up' makes the escort's profession very clear
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the collision of Liz's attempt to use an escort purely functionally (a ride home) with the reminder of what escorts actually do, via 'chlamydia flare-up.' The phrase 'chlamydia flare-up' is both specific enough to be real and ridiculous as a reason for a date cancellation.

jokes.text: Grizz and Dotcom are asked to 'pretend to be bouncers' for the TGS VIP room. Dotcom: 'Maybe someday we'll live in a world where you ask us to pretend to be scientists.'
jokes.setup: Jack thanks Grizz and Dotcom for pretending to be bouncers
jokes.punchline: Dotcom's hope for a world where large Black men are cast as scientists rather than bouncers is a meta-commentary on Hollywood racial typecasting, delivered with genuine feeling
jokes.explanation: A genuinely sharp joke that acknowledges racial typecasting while also being funny. Dotcom is established as one of the most intelligent characters on the show (he makes literary references, has multiple degrees), so his comment about wanting to be cast as a scientist is loaded with character history. The earnestness of 'maybe someday we'll live in a world' gives it weight beyond a simple race joke. Justifies 8+: strong character integration, smart meta-commentary, and the idealistic framing ('maybe someday') makes it resonant.

jokes.text: Ooh, she's getting the Jack Donaghy 'A' game. I hope she can keep her clothes on. / Lemon, your hair looks very nice today. You should wear it like that more often. / Oh, my. Well, I... never, uh...
jokes.setup: Liz sarcastically foreshadows Avery being undone by Jack's 'A' game.
jokes.punchline: Jack immediately demonstrates a fragment of the A game on Liz herself with a simple hair compliment — and Liz completely falls apart, implying that basic flattery is enough to undo even her defenses.
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural joke — Liz sets up the premise (Jack's A game undoes women), Jack demonstrates it on the nearest available subject, and Liz proves the hypothesis. The 'Oh, my. Well, I... never, uh...' reaction captures how easily her cynicism collapses under any genuine compliment. Strong character work for both.

jokes.text: Jenna holding Maynard's first letter: 'Jenna, I was in your bedroom last night. I left a gift in your toilet. You will be my bride someday.'
jokes.setup: Jenna tearfully shows Kenneth the first letter her stalker ever sent her — framed as a romantic keepsake
jokes.punchline: The letter is a threat, an act of bathroom vandalism, and a kidnapping pledge — and Jenna is devastated to have lost this man
jokes.explanation: Three escalating horrors in three sentences: breaking and entering, a 'gift in your toilet' (the vagueness is funnier than specificity), and a marriage threat. The joke is perfect because it's structured like a romantic letter (bed + gift + marriage pledge) but each element is the opposite of romantic. Kenneth's horrified reaction ('how can you be upset about losing a guy like this?') makes it land. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Kenneth: 'Oh, how can you be upset about losing a guy like this, Miss Maroney?'
jokes.setup: Jenna has just read a letter containing breaking-and-entering, toilet vandalism, and a kidnapping pledge
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's reaction is incredulity that she's sad — but it's ambiguous whether he's appalled by the letter or by her attachment to it; either way it's perfect
jokes.explanation: A good reaction beat that's ambiguous in the best way. Kenneth being horrified by the letter is the expected reading, but there's also a reading where Kenneth (in his innocent way) understands why a man's devotion would be compelling. The ambiguity is what makes it work.

jokes.text: 'He's the longest relationship I've ever had. Except, of course, for Doug.' / 'Please do not say what Doug is.' / 'Doug is my vibrator.'
jokes.setup: Jenna says the stalker was her longest relationship; Kenneth pleads with her not to reveal Doug's identity
jokes.punchline: Kenneth already knows what Doug is, making his 'please don't' funnier — and Jenna ignores him anyway
jokes.explanation: The structure is excellent: Kenneth already knows, begs her not to say it, she says it anyway. The 'please do not say what Doug is' is funnier than just setting up the revelation because it implies prior conversations of this nature. Kenneth's innocent demeanor makes oversharing about vibrators particularly uncomfortable.

jokes.text: Liz calls the doctor's office: 'I don't have anyone to pick me up. And I will be leaving alone.' / 'Ma'am, you really need someone.' / 'No, I don't. I don't need anyone. Because I can do every single thing that a person in a relationship can. Everything. Even zip up my own dress.'
jokes.setup: Liz declares her complete independence; the examples escalate to prove her point
jokes.punchline: 'Even zip up my own dress' — her climactic example of total self-sufficiency is so mundane it deflates the speech entirely
jokes.explanation: The structure is the joke: Liz builds to a triumphant declaration of independence, and the peak achievement is 'zip up my own dress.' The dress zipper has long been coded as a symbol of needing a partner, so using it as the climactic example inadvertently reveals exactly what she's missing. The fact that she includes 'even' before it suggests she knows it's the hardest thing. Excellent Liz Lemon character integration. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: The doctor's response: 'You know, there are some things that are actually harder to do with two people. Such as monologues.'
jokes.setup: Liz has just delivered a monologue about being able to do everything alone
jokes.punchline: The person on the phone responds with a deadpan observation that is (a) technically true and (b) a direct meta-reference to the fact that Liz just did a monologue
jokes.explanation: A quietly brilliant meta-joke. 'Such as monologues' simultaneously acknowledges that Liz just performed a monologue (meta), is technically true (monologues are easier to do alone), and serves as a gentle dismissal of her entire speech. The economy is excellent — the setup is Liz's entire tirade, and the punchline is four words. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Jon Bon Jovi asking 'Arena rock anthem, power ballad?' when Jack says he needs a favor for a date
jokes.setup: Jack tells Bon Jovi he has a date coming and needs his help
jokes.punchline: Bon Jovi immediately categorizes the request in his only terms of reference — musical genres — before Jack has said what he wants
jokes.explanation: A quick character beat that works through Bon Jovi's limited frame of reference — everything in his world is either an arena rock anthem or a power ballad. The speed of the question (before Jack has said what he needs) is what makes it funny.

jokes.text: Bon Jovi's response to being used as a prop: 'Oh, sure. That sounds like an appropriate use of my time and talent.'
jokes.setup: Jack asks Bon Jovi to just 'come over and say hello' to his date
jokes.punchline: Bon Jovi's sarcastic acquiescence — 'appropriate use of my time and talent' — is perfect celebrity self-awareness; he knows he's being used as a prop
jokes.explanation: Bon Jovi's self-deprecating willingness to be a party trick is funny because of the contrast with his actual stature. The formality of 'appropriate use of my time and talent' is deadpan perfection. Works well as celebrity-playing-against-type comedy.

jokes.text: Jon Bon Jovi reading the liability release aloud: 'I, the undersigned, henceforth known as "The Alone," hereby state that on February 14th, I have absolutely no one in my life.'
jokes.setup: Liz needs to sign a liability release to leave surgery alone; Jon Bon Jovi is reading it
jokes.punchline: The official legal document refers to the patient as 'The Alone' — the medical establishment has a formal designation for lonely Valentine's Day surgery patients
jokes.explanation: The legal terminology 'The Alone' as a formal designation is an inspired joke. The document's existence implies this is common enough to have standardized language. Also, the absurdity of Jon Bon Jovi reading this document to Liz Lemon layers in extra humor via the surreal celebrity context. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: The release continues: '"Jane Sadwoman" release Dr. Kaplan's office... Will likely die alone, eaten by house cats.'
jokes.setup: The legal document has already called Liz 'The Alone'; the document continues
jokes.punchline: 'Jane Sadwoman' as the alias AND 'will likely die alone, eaten by house cats' as the official medical prediction — the document has opinions
jokes.explanation: An escalation of an already excellent joke. 'Jane Sadwoman' as the legal alias and 'will likely die alone, eaten by house cats' as a formal medical opinion in a release form is absurdist escalation at its finest. The house cats detail is culturally specific (the single woman with cats trope) but the word 'likely' makes it even funnier — it's a probabilistic assessment. One of the episode's standout jokes. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Liz's plan after refusing to sign: 'I just tell them that my boyfriend is going to pick me up. And then, after the surgery, I'll make a run for it.'
jokes.setup: Liz refuses to sign the release on principle
jokes.punchline: Her plan is to invent a boyfriend, then sprint out of the surgery center while post-anesthesia — which is both impossible and perfectly Liz
jokes.explanation: The plan is obviously unworkable (she'll be post-anesthesia) but Liz states it with complete confidence. Character-specific — this is exactly the kind of panicked improvised plan Liz would devise.

jokes.text: Jon Bon Jovi's karaoke commercial: 'I'm Tyke Myson, baby boxer. I wrote that.'
jokes.setup: Jon Bon Jovi calls something the 'lamest thing' he's heard
jokes.punchline: He references a bizarre karaoke commercial featuring 'Tyke Myson, baby boxer' — and then admits he wrote it
jokes.explanation: The joke requires Bon Jovi playing himself as someone who wrote a ridiculous jingle about a 'baby boxer' named Tyke Myson — a play on Mike Tyson. The self-deprecation ('I wrote that') is funnier because Bon Jovi was genuinely famous. The name 'Tyke Myson' is a nice absurdist detail.

jokes.text: Because my boyfriend, Astronaut Mike Dexter, will be picking me up. On his motorcycle.
jokes.setup: Liz tells the doctor's office she doesn't need the release because her boyfriend will pick her up.
jokes.punchline: The name 'Astronaut Mike Dexter' is Liz's go-to fake boyfriend — an aspirational fantasy figure whose occupation (astronaut) and name (Mike Dexter, classic romance novel hero name) are maximally idealized.
jokes.explanation: 'Astronaut Mike Dexter' is arguably the most quotable character name in 30 Rock history. It perfectly captures Liz Lemon's idealized romantic fantasy — the combination of 'Astronaut' (maximum achievement/heroism) with 'Mike Dexter' (the platonic paperback romance hero name) is comedy writing at its best. The addition of 'on his motorcycle' is the perfect unnecessary detail. This name became a cultural shorthand.

jokes.text: Post-anesthesia Liz singing 'I Will Remember You' in the waiting room while Maynard — Jenna's stalker — is also there
jokes.setup: Liz is waiting post-surgery, ostensibly for her fake boyfriend
jokes.punchline: She's singing a Sarah McLachlan song in the waiting room, apparently not fully conscious; Jenna's stalker appears beside her
jokes.explanation: A sustained visual/physical comedy sequence — Liz singing in a waiting room while drugged, intercut with the lyrics on screen, is a tonal contrast joke (the earnestness of the song vs. the pathos of the situation). The appearance of Maynard creates a comedic collision of the two storylines.

jokes.text: 'I don't think the "anastacia" actually "affectored" me.' — Liz's post-anesthesia speech
jokes.setup: Liz emerges from surgery supposedly fine
jokes.punchline: She uses 'anastacia' for 'anesthesia' and 'affectored' for 'affected' in the same sentence, while believing she's speaking normally
jokes.explanation: The joke is that the anesthesia-induced malapropisms are dense in a single short sentence. 'Anastacia' (the pop singer) and 'affectored' (not a word) delivered with complete confidence is good physical/verbal comedy. The economy is nearly perfect — maximum information about her impairment in eight words.

jokes.text: Oh, my God. What are you doing here? / We knew you'd need a ride home. / What do you mean, 'we'?
jokes.setup: Liz wakes up post-surgery to find a surprise.
jokes.punchline: Her ex-boyfriends have all gathered to take her home — the answer to her Valentine's isolation is all the men she's loved, together in a waiting room.
jokes.explanation: Good structural payoff. The 'we' reveal is well-played and the warm-cringe combination of all exes gathered in one room is a classic sitcom construction. Sets up the anesthesia-vision sequence.

jokes.text: Post-anesthesia Liz to Drew: 'So handsome. So, so stupid.'
jokes.setup: Liz sees Drew among her rescuers and addresses him directly
jokes.punchline: Her assessment of Drew is perfect and compressed — and 'so, so stupid' delivered with the same reverence as 'so handsome' is the joke
jokes.explanation: Five words that perfectly summarize Drew as a character. The anesthesia allows Liz to say what she actually thinks; 'so, so stupid' as a loving addition to 'so handsome' is both a callback to the Drew character (who was established as spectacularly beautiful and dim) and a genuine affectionate character beat. Near-perfect economy. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: 'I am a sailor on the sea of the human heart.'
jokes.setup: Liz is wrapping up her anesthesia-fueled romantic speech
jokes.punchline: The metaphor is so overblown and purple that it becomes the joke — Liz's drugged brain has produced a terrible inspirational poster
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the gap between Liz's normal sardonic voice and this grandiose drugged declaration. 'Sailor on the sea of the human heart' is exactly what an anesthesia-addled person would think is profound. High quotability because it's so gloriously overwritten.

jokes.text: Jack: 'Okay, this bitch is tripping her ass off.' / 'What do we do with her?' / 'I got a date tonight. I say we order her some pizza.' / 'Yes!' / 'and lock her in here for the weekend.'
jokes.setup: Liz has just given an overwrought drugged speech; the group assesses the situation
jokes.punchline: Jack's unsentimental assessment ('this bitch is tripping') followed by a vote to abandon her for the weekend with pizza is a comic deflation of the emotional moment — and Jack calling her a bitch is so out of character it's its own joke
jokes.explanation: The tonal pivot from Liz's earnest drugged monologue to Jack's clinical 'this bitch is tripping her ass off' is a perfect comedic deflation. The vote to 'order her some pizza and lock her in here for the weekend' is absurd enough to be funny and just believable enough given the characters. Jack's 'I got a date tonight' as his primary concern is excellent character comedy.

jokes.text: Liz, still drugged, to Bon Jovi on the phone: 'What's that, Bon Jovi? You love me too?'
jokes.setup: Liz is calling people from her phone while fully drugged
jokes.punchline: She has apparently called Jon Bon Jovi and is hallucinating a two-way conversation about love
jokes.explanation: A good callback that completes the Bon Jovi running thread. The image of drugged Liz calling Bon Jovi and hallucinating his reciprocal love is sweet and absurd in equal measure. Works as a capper for the Bon Jovi subplot.

jokes.text: Hey, do you want to grab breakfast? / You're sweet, Jack. But let's not pretend this is anything more than it is.
jokes.setup: Jack suggests continuing their relationship after the night together.
jokes.punchline: Avery reverses the typical gender dynamic — she's the one delivering the 'let's not make this more than it is' speech that men usually give. She's the commitment-phobe.
jokes.explanation: The role reversal is the joke — Jack, who explicitly said he wanted 'something fun and easy' and 'a win,' is now the one wanting commitment while Avery delivers the classic morning-after brush-off. Good character inversion.

jokes.text: Jack: 'A son I can throw a ball to and, when he's older, have power struggles with.'
jokes.setup: Jack is insisting he wants a family and describes his ideal child
jokes.punchline: His vision of fatherhood skips past love/nurturing and goes directly to 'power struggles' as the endpoint of the father-son relationship
jokes.explanation: The joke is in what Jack omits from his family vision (love, warmth, connection) and what he includes ('power struggles'). The escalation from normal fatherly activity (throwing a ball) to 'power struggles' reveals Jack's competitive soul. High character integration — this is definitively Jack Donaghy's vision of family.

jokes.text: Jack on the phone: 'I need to go.' / Avery: 'Jack, the phone trick again?' / 'This isn't a trick. I have to pick up a hallucinating employee of mine from the oral surgeon's office.' / 'Well, that's at least creative.'
jokes.setup: Avery assumes Jack is using the fake conference call trick again
jokes.punchline: The truth (picking up a hallucinating employee from a dentist) sounds more implausible than the original lie, so she thinks he's being creative
jokes.explanation: An elegant structural callback: the truth sounds like a lie because it's more absurd than the original fake. 'That's at least creative' from Avery is a perfect response — she's half-convinced, which is all Jack needs. The plot mechanics and comedy are serving each other well here.

jokes.text: Jack: 'Cancel your walk of shame. Come with me on a car ride of proof.'
jokes.setup: Jack is trying to convince Avery to come with him to pick up Liz
jokes.punchline: 'Walk of shame' vs. 'car ride of proof' — a parallel construction that upgrades a typically embarrassing event into a demonstration of Jack's trustworthiness
jokes.explanation: A highly quotable line with excellent construction. 'Walk of shame / car ride of proof' is a perfectly parallel rhetorical construction that also advances the plot and reveals character (Jack is always framing everything as strategy). The economy is near-perfect: seven words that do four things at once. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Jenna finds the 'gift' of having her car vandalized: 'Oh, my God! Who did this?' / Kenneth: 'I don't know. I guess some weirdo out there loves you.'
jokes.setup: Jenna is mourning the loss of her stalker
jokes.punchline: Her car has been vandalized — presumably by the stalker as a parting gift — and Kenneth characterizes it as love
jokes.explanation: A good closing beat for the Jenna/Maynard subplot. Kenneth's framing of car vandalism as love ('some weirdo out there loves you') is appropriately sad and sweet and wrong all at once. The callback to Jenna's need for validation lands.

jokes.text: Thank you, Kenneth. / I don't know what you're talking about. / Happy Valentine's Day.
jokes.setup: Jenna thanks Kenneth for the Valentine's gesture.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth denies it while wishing her Happy Valentine's Day — the denial and affirmation in the same breath is a sweet-deadpan combination.
jokes.explanation: Efficient and warm Kenneth character moment. The denial/well-wishing juxtaposition is simple but effective.

jokes.text: What hotel is this? / Would you just keep an eye on her? I'm going to turn down her bed. / I was sure he was making this up.
jokes.setup: Jack has brought Avery along to collect the hallucinating Liz.
jokes.punchline: Avery, who doubted the story was real, witnesses the truth and acknowledges she was wrong — with Liz's confused question about 'what hotel' confirming the anesthesia's extent.
jokes.explanation: Good callback payoff — Liz thinking she's in a hotel while post-surgery is consistent with her altered state. Avery's admission that she was wrong about Jack making it up is a nice character beat.

jokes.text: Liz, still drugged in bed, talking to Avery: 'Yes, you're a very pretty doggie.'
jokes.setup: Avery has come along to help with Liz; Liz is still post-anesthesia
jokes.punchline: Liz mistakes or speaks to Avery as a dog — confirming she's still completely impaired
jokes.explanation: A functional post-anesthesia joke. Liz calling a very composed TV anchor a 'pretty doggie' is funny through the juxtaposition but not especially original. Works as a visual beat.

jokes.text: No, no, no, no, no, no. Lemon, it's time for bed. It's time for bed.
jokes.setup: Liz is doing something unspecified and alarming post-surgery.
jokes.punchline: Jack's urgent, repeated 'no no no no no' and parental 'it's time for bed' suggests Liz is doing something chaotic or embarrassing that we can only imagine.
jokes.explanation: The unexplained alarm in Jack's voice is funnier than anything specific — the audience's imagination supplies the content. Jack's parental authority over a drugged Liz is a good character moment.

jokes.text: The final scene: two women at a restaurant, one says 'Don Cheadle on a bed of rice.' The other: 'No, she didn't. She didn't.'
jokes.setup: Two women discussing Valentine's Day loneliness; one asks what to order for lunch
jokes.punchline: 'Don Cheadle on a bed of rice' as a lunch order — framing the actor as a meal — is surreal and the friend's delighted reaction ('No, she didn't!') confirms it as a joke about sexual fantasy
jokes.explanation: A wonderfully absurdist final joke. Ordering 'Don Cheadle on a bed of rice' as a lunch item is a perfect blend of fantasy and mundanity — the 'bed of rice' makes it sound like an actual menu item. The friend's reaction ('No, she didn't!') sells it as transgressive humor while keeping it playful. High quotability and a memorable episode-closer. Justifies the craft score: the specificity of 'on a bed of rice' is what elevates this above a simple celebrity crush joke.

jokes.text: Final line to camera: 'Happy Valentine's Day, no one.'
jokes.setup: The episode has been about loneliness on Valentine's Day
jokes.punchline: Addressing the audience/nobody as 'no one' is the perfect capper — simultaneously addressing anyone who might be watching alone AND confirming her own solitude
jokes.explanation: Four words that function as both the episode's closing joke and its thematic statement. 'Happy Valentine's Day, no one' is addressing the camera/audience, which implies the viewer is also 'no one' — the joke includes the audience in the loneliness. The economy is perfect: maximum payload in minimum words. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: You see how she try to act like she don't want one? Uh-huh. You know she going to come back in here crying when she can't kill a water bug.
jokes.setup: Shanice's friend is skeptical of her independence claim.
jokes.punchline: The prediction that Shanice will return crying when she can't kill a water bug reduces the independence debate to its most mundane possible test case.
jokes.explanation: The water bug as the ultimate test of independence is a genuinely funny specific detail — it's both stereotypically domestic and genuinely terrifying (water bugs are horrible). Good observational comedy about urban apartment life.

tmdb_overview: Liz schedules a root canal to avoid feeling lonely on Valentine's Day; Jack woos an attractive and successful TV host; Jenna's stalker loses interest.
insight: Liz's feminist holiday spirals into 209 seconds of pure character-driven cringe.
